title: Memoization Strategies
description: Apply memoization techniques to prevent redundant React Query executions and unnecessary re-renders.

data.text: React Query does an impressive amount of memoization internally: it deduplicates requests, caches by reference, and uses structural sharing to avoid re-rendering when data has not changed. But in complex UIs, you still need to apply **memoization strategies** at the component and hook level to prevent expensive re-renders and redundant computations.

React Query memoizes query results by default. When a query resolves, the result is cached. If another component requests the same query key, React Query returns the cached reference. If a background refetch returns identical data, structural sharing ensures React sees the same object reference and skips re-rendering.

data.title: Structural Sharing by Default
data.text: React Query compares each key in the new response with the old one. If a value has not changed by reference, it reuses the old reference. This is why updating one field in a large object does not re-render every consumer.

data.caption: How React Query structural sharing prevents unnecessary re-renders
data.definition:
graph TB
    A[Old Cache Object] --> B{Compare keys by reference}
    C[New Fetch Response] --> B
    B -->|Same reference| D[Reuse old object]
    B -->|Changed reference| E[Create new cached object]
    D --> F[No re-render]
    E --> G[Re-render only changed consumers]

data.text: When you derive data from a query â€” sorting a list, filtering items, or computing aggregates â€” the derivation runs on every render by default. Wrap expensive derivations in `useMemo` so they only recalculate when the underlying query data changes.

data.content: Using useMemo to prevent expensive list transformations on every render

data.text: Passing inline functions to memoized child components breaks their memoization because the function reference changes on every render. Use `useCallback` for event handlers and query functions that depend on props or state.

data.content: Generating dynamic query keys without breaking referential equality

data.title: Memoization Decision Guide
items: Use useMemo for filtering, sorting, or mapping large arrays
Use useCallback for handlers passed to memoized children (React.memo)
Avoid memoizing simple values like strings or booleans
Avoid wrapping everything in useMemo/useCallback by default
Profile first to confirm a performance problem exists

data.title: Optimize a Dashboard with Memoization
data.description: You have a dashboard with three widgets that all consume the same query. When the user types in a search box, the entire dashboard re-renders. Apply memoization so only the relevant widget updates.
steps: Identify the expensive computations in each widget (filtering, sorting, formatting)
Wrap each computation in useMemo with the correct dependency array
Wrap the refresh callback in useCallback so the QueryClient reference is stable
Verify with React DevTools Profiler that widgets outside the search scope do not re-render
data.expectedOutcome: Only the search widget re-renders on keystroke. Other widgets remain stable.

data.title: Profile before you memoize
data.text: Use React DevTools Profiler to confirm a component is re-rendering unnecessarily. Premature memoization adds complexity without measurable benefit.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: React Query structural sharing prevents re-renders when data is unchanged
Use useMemo for expensive derivations like filtering and sorting
Use useCallback for event handlers passed to memoized children
Profile first to ensure memoization solves a real problem
data.takeaway: Memoization is most effective when applied deliberately to known bottlenecks, not everywhere by default.
